title: Heap Operations: Insert, Extract, and Build-Heap
summary: Every heap operation reduces to two primitives, sift-up and sift-down, which also combine into an O(n) build-heap and an in-place heap sort.

slides.markdown:
Everything a binary heap does — insert, remove the min/max, or build itself from scratch — reduces to two moves: **sift-up** (bubble a value toward the root) and **sift-down** (push a value toward the leaves).

Insert is append-then-sift-up. Extract-root is swap-then-shrink-then-sift-down. Build-heap from an unsorted array is a clever reuse of sift-down that runs in O(n), not the O(n log n) you'd expect from n inserts. Heap sort is build-heap plus repeated extraction.

Master these two primitives and you've implemented the entire structure — [binary-heap-fundamentals](binary-heap-fundamentals) covered the shape; this topic covers the mechanism.

To insert a value, append it to the **end of the array** — the next open leaf slot, which is exactly where completeness says the new node belongs. That new leaf almost certainly violates the heap property against its parent, so **sift-up** repairs it: compare the new element to its parent, and if it's smaller (min-heap), swap them. Repeat from the new position until the parent is smaller or you reach the root.

Because the tree has height at most floor(log2 n), sift-up does at most that many swaps — **O(log n)** per insert. The append itself is an amortized O(1) dynamic-array operation, so it never dominates.

Notice what *doesn't* move: everything below the inserted leaf, and every node not on the direct path from the new leaf to the root, stays untouched.

```python
def sift_up(heap, i):
    while i > 0:
        parent = (i - 1) // 2
        if heap[i] < heap[parent]:      # min-heap: flip for max-heap
            heap[i], heap[parent] = heap[parent], heap[i]
            i = parent
        else:
            break                        # heap property restored
    return heap
```

The loop terminates the moment the current node is no longer smaller than its parent — that early `break` is what keeps the cost proportional to how far the value actually needs to travel, not always the full height. An element inserted near its correct spot might do zero swaps; only a new global minimum travels all the way to the root.

Removing the root (the min or max) can't just delete index 0 — that would leave a hole and break the array's completeness. Instead:

1. Save the root's value to return.
2. Move the **last element** in the array into the root's slot.
3. Shrink the array by one (drop the now-duplicated last slot).
4. **Sift-down** the new root into place, since it's almost certainly too big to sit there.

Moving the last leaf into the root is what keeps the tree complete after removal — it's the mirror image of insert's "append at the next open leaf." The heavy lifting is entirely in step 4, and — like sift-up — it costs at most O(log n) because it only ever travels one root-to-leaf path.

A node can have **zero, one, or two children** — the last level of a complete tree is filled left to right and may stop partway through. Sift-down has to handle the one-child case correctly, or it silently produces an invalid heap.

The bug: comparing against `right` when `right` is out of bounds (`right >= size`), reading garbage or a stale value from a previous, larger heap size. The fix — visible in the sift-down code above — is guarding every child comparison with a bounds check (`left < size`, `right < size`) **before** comparing values, never comparing unconditionally and hoping the index happens to be valid.

This edge case is exactly where interview heap implementations most often fail on a hidden test case: a heap of even size, sifting down a node whose last-level child is missing on one side.

Given an unsorted array, you don't need to insert elements one at a time. **Build-heap** instead calls sift-down on every **internal node**, starting from the *last* one and working backward to the root.

An internal node is any node with at least one child — its index runs from `(n // 2) - 1` down to `0`. Leaves (everything past that) are already trivially valid one-node heaps, so there's nothing to sift.

```python
def build_heap(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    for i in range(n // 2 - 1, -1, -1):
        sift_down(arr, i, n)
    return arr
```

Processing bottom-up guarantees that by the time you sift-down a node, both its child subtrees are already valid heaps — exactly the precondition sift-down requires.

slides.sectionTitle: Why build-heap is linear, not n·log n
slides.markdown:
It looks like n/2 calls to sift-down, each costing up to O(log n), so O(n log n) — but that overcounts badly, because **most nodes are near the bottom**, where sift-down barely does any work.

The honest bound sums each node's cost by its height, not by the tree's total height:

- Half the nodes are leaves → 0 sift-down work.
- A quarter are one level up → at most 1 swap each.
- An eighth are two levels up → at most 2 swaps each.
- ...and so on, geometrically shrinking.

That sum, `n/2·0 + n/4·1 + n/8·2 + ...`, converges to **O(n)** — a classic case of a geometric series beating the naive per-call worst case. This is the single most-cited "surprising" complexity result in the heap topic, and interviewers routinely ask you to justify it rather than just state it.

Both approaches end with a valid heap over n elements, but the bound genuinely differs:

| | Build-heap (bottom-up sift-down) | n sequential inserts |
|---|---|---|
| Total cost | O(n) | O(n log n) worst case |
| Why | most nodes are near leaves, doing near-zero work | every insert can cost up to O(log n), and the tree is already near full height for most of the inserts |
| When it applies | you have the *whole* array upfront | elements arrive one at a time, over time |

If you're handed a full array and need a heap immediately — say, seeding K-way merge with one array per source — always call build-heap, never insert one by one. If elements genuinely arrive over time (a live event stream), insertion is the only option anyway, and the O(log n)-per-insert cost is unavoidable.

Heap sort combines both primitives: build a max-heap, then repeatedly swap the root (the current max) to the end of the shrinking array and sift-down the new root.

```python
def heap_sort(arr):
    n = len(arr)
    build_max_heap(arr)                 # O(n)
    for end in range(n - 1, 0, -1):
        arr[0], arr[end] = arr[end], arr[0]
        sift_down(arr, 0, end)          # heap size shrinks to `end`
    return arr
```

Each of the n-1 extractions costs O(log n), for O(n log n) total — matching merge sort's bound, but **in place**, with O(1) auxiliary space versus merge sort's O(n) buffer. That's heap sort's real selling point: a guaranteed O(n log n) worst case with no extra memory, at the cost of poor cache locality (covered as a trade-off in [comparing-classic-sorts](comparing-classic-sorts)).

Heap sort's in-place swaps are efficient, but they mean **the array is no longer a valid heap the moment sorting finishes** — and it isn't even a valid heap *during* the process past the shrinking boundary, since the sorted suffix now holds final values that no longer participate in sift-down at all.

A subtler version of the same mistake: forgetting that `sift_down`'s effective heap size must shrink on every iteration (the `end` parameter above). Sift-down against the *original* array length after elements have already been placed at the tail causes it to compare against and potentially disturb values that are already in their final sorted position — silently producing a wrong sort that looks almost right.

If you need both a sorted array **and** a live heap afterward, you need two separate structures — heap sort consumes the heap to produce the sort.
